label: Person
name: Adriano Castellesi
summary:
Adriano Castellesi (c. 1461–c. 1521) was an Italian cardinal, humanist scholar, and papal diplomat who served as an agent of the English crown at the Vatican before his career collapsed spectacularly in connection with the alleged conspiracy to poison Pope Leo X. Born in Corneto (modern Tarquinia), he became a significant figure in the Renaissance humanist network connecting the Italian courts with the English Lancastrian and early Tudor courts.

Castellesi served as papal tax collector (nuncio) in England from 1490 and became Bishop of Hereford (1502) and then Bath and Wells (1504), accumulating English benefices in absentia while residing in Rome as a humanist scholar and courtier. He was made a cardinal in 1503 by Pope Julius II. His Latin literary work 'De vera philosophia' was respected by Erasmus, placing him among the serious humanist scholars of the Renaissance cardinalate.

His career ended in disaster: implicated in the alleged plot to poison Leo X in 1517, he was stripped of his cardinalate and fled Rome. He was last documented alive in Venice in 1521, and the circumstances of his death remain uncertain — possibly murdered by his own servant. His career exemplifies the Renaissance cardinalate's combination of genuine scholarly accomplishment, political intrigue, and personal ambition.

causes: Renaissance papacy's diplomatic needs required educated Italian humanists who could serve as nuncios and tax collectors at foreign courts
Henry VII and Henry VIII's England needed skilled intermediaries with the papacy for diplomatic and ecclesiastical business
Renaissance cardinalate's culture of patronage and scholarship rewarded humanists like Castellesi with high ecclesiastical office
effects: His English diplomatic service and absentee benefices exemplify the pre-Tridentine Church's abuse of non-residency that reformers attacked
His connection with Erasmus demonstrates the Renaissance humanist network's reach across national boundaries
His disgrace in the alleged Leo X poisoning plot illustrates the dangerous political environment of the Renaissance papacy
His fate — stripped of cardinalate and dying obscurely — demonstrates the Renaissance court's ruthlessness
